69.0.0.en: 1- Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul.

69.0.1.en: 1- David feels that sorrows have increased upon him, so that they became like waters that rose until they covered his whole body up to his neck and nearly drowned him. Therefore he asks God for salvation, to lift these events from him, since his tribe Judah was slow to bring him back to his throne, at the very time when it ought to have been the first of the tribes to be blamed for this; for Jerusalem lies in the tribe of Judah, while the rest of the tribes wanted to bring him back, and an expected conflict arose between the tribes and the tribe of Judah. All this while David was driven out, a stranger to his city Jerusalem, far from the ark of the covenant of God, and suffering because of what Absalom had done to him, and the betrayal of many. Therefore he asked God to save him from all these psychological troubles, in addition to the bodily troubles, since he was not living honored as a king.

69.0.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, upon whom sorrows gathered in the last week of His life, especially when He was praying in the garden of Gethsemane before He was arrested.

69.0.3.en: 3- This verse is also a prophecy about the Babylonian captivity, for these are the feelings of the Jews at their captivity. It is also a prophecy about the prophet Jonah, for these are his feelings while in the belly of the whale.

69.1.0.en: 2- I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.

69.1.1.en: Floods: a strong current of water.

69.1.2.en: 1- David depicts the extent of his sufferings as though he had sunk in deep mud and could not find a place for his feet to stand, but sinks endlessly, that is, he is exposed to destruction. Then he depicts himself as having entered deep waters, with strong currents of water covering him, so that he nearly drowned; so also are his sorrows and sufferings, especially since he finds no way out of them and no support to lean on, and there was nothing left before him but God his Savior.

69.1.3.en: 2- This is also a prophecy about Christ, in the last week of His life, sunk in His sorrows and sufferings for the redemption of humanity.

69.2.0.en: 3- I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.

69.2.2.en: 1- David expresses his many pains that took in all his members: his feet find no place to stand, as in the previous verse, and in this verse we find that his throat is weary and dry and he is no longer able to continue crying out. As for his eyes, they have grown weary from looking so much to God, while He is slow and does not answer. This verse expresses the extent of David's sorrows and his great need of God. It is a kind of entreaty and insistence upon God to have compassion on him.

69.2.3.en: 2- Perhaps this verse depicts part of the sufferings of Christ on the cross, where His throat dried, as He said, "I thirst," and His eyes grew weary as He bore the cup of God's wrath on behalf of humanity, and asked that the cup pass from Him, and it did not pass, and He completed the redemption to redeem us by His wonderful love.

69.3.0.en: 4- They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head: they that would destroy me, being mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty: then I restored that which I took not away.

69.3.1.en: 1- David shows the great number of those who wronged him and hated him, saying that they are more than the hairs of his head, and that they tried to consume him with their many evils in order to be rid of him, and in all this he was wronged and had done no evil, and he restored to them what he had not seized, namely the throne of the kingdom; for God was the one who anointed him by the hand of Samuel, and the people made him king. Those who rose up against David were so many that it is hard to count them, such as Shimei the son of Gera and Ahithophel.

69.3.2.en: 2- This verse also applies to Christ, against whom the Jewish people, the scribes and the Pharisees rose up, and tried to ensnare Him in errors but were unable, and He restored what He had not seized, for He was crucified as a sin offering for us though He had not sinned, and He restored Adam, whom Satan had seized and made fall into sin, and brought him back to Paradise.

69.3.3.en: If you suffer pains and sorrows, know that your Christ suffered before you, though He did not err, so ask His help and He will support you, and even compensate you for what you have borne with abundant blessings.

69.4.0.en: 5- O God, thou knowest my foolishness; and my sins are not hid from thee.

69.4.1.en: Although David declared in the previous verses that he was wronged and exposed to many troubles, he returns and confesses his foolishness and sins. There is no contradiction between this verse and the previous verses, because there is no person without sin, whether voluntary sins, even if few, in addition to the sins he commits without knowledge and in ignorance. This shows two things:

69.4.2.en: 1- David's carefulness and his repentance of every sin.

69.4.3.en: 2- David's humility in declaring his weakness by saying "my foolishness"; for if God charges His angels with folly, how much more do human beings fall into various follies.

69.5.0.en: 6- Let not them that wait on thee, O Lord God of hosts, be ashamed for my sake: let not those that seek thee be confounded for my sake, O God of Israel.

69.5.1.en: 7- Because for thy sake I have borne reproach; shame hath covered my face. 8- I am become a stranger unto my brethren, and an alien unto my mother's children.

69.5.2.en: 1- While David was suffering and bearing the pains of being driven out of Jerusalem and exposed to death, his heart took pity on all who believe in God, and who see in King David an example for themselves, lest they doubt the way of righteousness and leave God. He enjoys God's care for him and is spiritually satisfied, but with a wonderful fatherhood he has compassion on his children, that is, his people, lest they stumble because of the following:

69.5.3.en: a- The shame and disgrace that covered David in his fleeing barefoot from the face of Absalom, and people's reproaching him, such as the reproach of Shimei the son of Gera (2 Sam 16:7, 8).

69.5.4.en: b- His brothers the Jews treated him with contempt, indeed with enmity, and considered him as though he were a foreigner and stranger to them, and rose up in a great army to destroy him and all who were with him.

69.5.5.en: 2- These verses apply to Christ, who bore the disgrace and shame of the cross and the false accusations directed at Him, but He asks the Father not to allow all who await the coming Messiah to stumble; so that if they see Him in weakness they do not doubt Him, but learn from Him endurance, and love for those who wrong them.

69.6.0.en: 9- For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me.

69.6.1.en: 1- Although David was driven out of Jerusalem, his heart was attached to the house of the Lord, that is, the tabernacle in which was the ark of the covenant, and he is zealous for the house of the Lord with a good zeal and fears that the wicked may wrong this house; indeed he longs to be beside the house of the Lord every day, to offer holy worship to God.

69.6.2.en: 2- Everyone who resists God and whose heart is filled with evil reproached David and resisted him, because he walks in uprightness; in addition, everyone who resisted God, or reproached Him, grieved David, because David was attached to God and did not want anyone to wrong the name of God.

69.6.3.en: 3- The zeal of God's house ate up the heart of Christ, so He drove the sellers out of the Temple, and said, "My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves" (Mt 21:13), in addition to His bearing many reproaches and accusations from the Jews and the priests. All this He accepted for our salvation and redemption.

69.7.0.en: 10- When I wept, and chastened my soul with fasting, that was to my reproach. 11- I made sackcloth also my garment; and I became a proverb to them.

69.7.1.en: Sackcloth: coarse garments worn in self-abasement before God.

69.7.2.en: 1- David makes clear what he bore of the toils of spiritual striving, and they are:

69.7.3.en: a- Weeping with prayers before God, which carries the meaning of repentance, and asking for help and salvation.

69.7.4.en: b- Fasting and abasing himself before God, but David's enemies considered his weeping and fasting weakness and disgrace, yet he did not care about their opinions, and held fast to his striving for the sake of God.

69.7.5.en: c- Wearing sackcloth and abasing himself before God after his fall into sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and after she bore him a child and it fell sick and was exposed to death (2 Sam 12:16, 17).

69.7.6.en: d- David became a proverb to those around him, who mocked him, and he bore them. And he was a type and symbol of Christ.

69.7.7.en: All this shows the extent of David's faithfulness in his spiritual striving, and his bearing the reproaches of his enemies.

69.7.8.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who grieved over Jerusalem (Mt 23:37) and fasted forty days, and put on our body, which was to Him like sackcloth, and became a byword of mockery and shame at His crucifixion; all this He bore for our salvation.

69.8.0.en: 12- They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards.

69.8.1.en: 1- After David had been the king sitting on the throne and the judge who governs his people, he was changed into a man driven out of the city, judged by the elders sitting beside the gate in the city square, that is, he became weak and accused, his case examined, although in truth he was innocent, and moreover the drunkards began to mock him with songs full of derision.

69.8.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, whom the scribes, the Pharisees and the chief priests accused with many false accusations, and tried at the end of His life on earth, and the soldiers, drunk with sin, mocked Him, and so they reviled the Lord of glory who is without sin.

69.8.3.en: If you are liable to fall into various sins, then at least offer repentance with striving and self-abasement before God, and He will lift them from you, and even comfort your heart and bring you back to His embrace.

69.9.0.en: 13- But as for me, my prayer is unto thee, O Lord, in an acceptable time: O God, in the multitude of thy mercy hear me, in the truth of thy salvation.

69.9.1.en: 1- Before all the afflictions that faced David, he could do nothing but direct his prayer to God with humility and self-abasement. This is what God asks, in order to be pleased with a person; for He loves the humble who cry to Him, and His mercies overflow upon them and He answers them.

69.9.2.en: 2- Christ also prayed in the garden of Gethsemane with humility and fervor, and then offered Himself as a sacrifice on the cross for us; all this pleased the Father, and He answered Him and accepted His sacrifice, and by His death He redeemed us and we received great mercies.

69.10.0.en: 14- Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink: let me be delivered from them that hate me, and out of the deep waters. 15- Let not the waterflood overflow me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me.

69.10.1.en: 1- David asks God to deliver him from the mire so that he may not sink and drown in it, and from the waters so that he may not fall into their depths and drown. What is meant by the mire and water is the wicked who hate David and try to destroy him though he is innocent. His request for deliverance also includes that God keep him in righteousness so that he is not led along with the wicked in their evil. And consequently, in the end, he does not enter the pit and have it close its mouth upon him, that is, he does not come out of it forever; for he has hope in the awaited Messiah, who is able to bring him out of the pit and lift him up to Paradise.

69.10.2.en: 2- These two verses apply to Christ, for the mire and water mean the sins that Christ bore for us, that is, the sins of all humanity, and because of them He was crucified and died, and went down to the pit, that is, Hades. But the pit could not hold Him, but He brought out Adam and his children, and all who died in hope, and brought them up to Paradise.

69.11.0.en: 16- Hear me, O Lord; for thy lovingkindness is good: turn unto me according to the multitude of thy tender mercies. 17- And hide not thy face from thy servant; for I am in trouble: hear me speedily. 18- Draw nigh unto my soul, and redeem it: deliver me because of mine enemies. 19- Thou hast known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonour: mine adversaries are all before thee.

69.11.1.en: 1- David pleads with God to include him in His mercies, because he suffers the pains of his sins and the pains of his enemies' harassment of him, so he urges God to answer him. He feels his weakness and unworthiness, but his hope is the mercies of God.

69.11.2.en: 2- From the intensity of his remorse David entreats God not to hide His face from him, as he feels that he is very sinful and does not deserve God's love and care, but feels that sin has bound him and he needs God to loose him from it, and set him free, indeed redeem him, that is, take his sins away from him. He believes in Christ the Redeemer who was to come in the fullness of time, and he is also confident that God knows everything, his sins and his enemies' harassment of him. So he asks Him in faith to intervene and have mercy on him and lift all these pains from him.

69.11.3.en: 3- These verses are about Christ, who bore our sins on His cross, and asks the Father to take them from Him, expressing the hideousness of sin and His distress over it, as He asked in the garden of Gethsemane that the cup of suffering pass from Him.

69.12.0.en: 20- Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none.

69.12.1.en: 21- They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

69.12.3.en: 1- David expresses his suffering from the shame that came upon him when Absalom drove him out, and even lay with his wives on the roof of his palace in front of all the people, and this shame was so heavy upon David that he became sick. David waited for a retreat from Absalom, but found even his counselors such as Ahithophel standing against him, so he found no comfort and no tender feelings; because of all these pains he asks God's mercies.

69.12.4.en: 2- As for Christ, the shame of the cross was heavy upon Him, and He passed through the winepress alone and found no comfort and no tender feelings from anyone; indeed, even in His thirst they gave Him vinegar mixed with bitterness and gall. This verse (v. 21) applies to Christ, and applies symbolically to David, as he bore sufferings like the bitterness of gall.

69.12.5.en: Sin binds your life, so do not be dazzled by its beauty, and do not slip running after its pleasure, and if you fall into it hasten to God with self-abasement, for He is merciful, and a tender Father ready to accept your repentance and free you from it, so that you return to your first sonship to God. Hold fast to your prayers and readings, and above all the sacraments of the Church, and you will remain steadfast in the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

69.13.0.en: 22- Let their table before them become a snare, and a trap for the secure.

69.13.1.en: Trap: a snare or a trap.

69.13.2.en: 1- The wicked caused the righteous man many troubles and gave him bitter drink and vinegar (v. 21); therefore he says here a prophecy of what will happen to them, meaning the Jews who rose up against Christ and crucified Him, that their table will become a snare. That is, their goods occupy them and keep them away from God. And as the hunter puts out food so that the animal falls into his net, so the devil uses their table and their material preoccupations to keep them away from God, and God permits this because they persisted in their sin, which is the torturing of the righteous man, by whom is meant Christ, or David who is a type of Him. And while they are secure and at ease they fall into the trap.

69.13.3.en: 2- The Jews sought the help of the Romans and their authority and crucified Christ, but the Romans became a snare for them, and besieged Jerusalem and destroyed it in AD 70. St. Paul the Apostle made clear that these verses are a prophecy about the Jews who crucified Christ (Rom 11:9, 10).

69.13.4.en: 3- The Holy Bible is the spiritual food, and the Jews did not understand the Holy Bible and all its prophecies about the Messiah, so they rejected Jesus Christ; that is, the word of God became a snare for them, so they rose up against Christ and crucified Him. They continued offering sacrifices after Christ had completed the redemption on the cross, so their table, that is, their altar on which they offer their sacrifices, became a snare that keeps them from faith in Christ, the true Sacrifice for us, to whom these sacrifices point.

69.14.0.en: 23- Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not; and make their loins continually to shake.

69.14.2.en: 1- If the righteous man's eyes grew weary from waiting for the Lord because of all he suffers from the wicked (v. 3), God punishes the wicked by darkening their eyes so that they do not see, that is, they lose the ability to discern. The Jews did not discern that Jesus is the awaited Messiah, although after Christ not one prophet appeared among the Jewish people; for the prophets were preparing the way and prophesying about the awaited Messiah, indeed their eyes were darkened at the hour of the cross when darkness came over all the earth.

69.14.3.en: 2- When a person is tired from work he feels pains in his back and needs sleep and rest, but the wicked have backs that remain in continual pain and trembling; because their inner anxiety causes them bodily pains, and these wicked, like the Jews who scourged Christ on His back and crucified Him, lived afterward in turmoil.

69.14.4.en: 3- These verses may seem to be wishing evil on the wicked, but David here states truths and prophecies about the Jews who would crucify Christ. It is a warning hundreds of years before the event, perhaps that they might repent.

69.15.0.en: 24- Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them. 25- Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents.

69.15.2.en: David prophesies about the Jews who crucified Christ and about Judas Iscariot, and about the wicked on the day of judgment, so he asks God to punish them with His intense anger and to lay waste their houses so that they have no rest and no stability. This is what happened in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and also in the death of Judas by a hideous death. As for the day of judgment, the punishment cannot be imagined from its dreadfulness. All this is to put the fear of God into the hearts of all, that they may repent and return to God, and He lift His anger from them.

69.16.0.en: 26- For they persecute him whom thou hast smitten; and they talk to the grief of those whom thou hast wounded.

69.16.1.en: 1- God permitted David to be smitten, that is, to suffer pains, so that he would be strengthened and become strong and able to govern and lead his country as king. But Saul rose up against him, and pursued him and tried to kill him, so Saul by his evil carried out the will of God, which was the smiting of David, yet he is called to account and punished for his evil. Those who shared with David while he was driven out from the face of Saul also were exposed to the same troubles of being driven out from the face of Saul and attempts to kill them, so they speak with grief, that is, with sorrow, of all they met from Saul's pursuit of them.

69.16.2.en: 2- This verse applies to Christ, whom it pleased the Father to bruise with grief (Isa 53:10), so He smote Him with the bearing of the bitter sins of the world on the cross. And the Jews drove Him out from among them by trying to ensnare Him with a word, and by the attempt to kill Him that ended with His crucifixion. And the disciples of Christ and all His followers were exposed to many pains and persecutions from the Jews, and they tell us with grief of all these persecutions, as appears from the Book of Acts and the history of the Church.

69.17.0.en: 27- Add iniquity unto their iniquity: and let them not come into thy righteousness. 28- Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.

69.17.1.en: 1- David asks God to gather the iniquities of the wicked who persecute the righteous. For the wicked persisted in their evil, and wronged not only the righteous man, but his followers.

69.17.2.en: 2- David also asks that these wicked be punished by not entering into the righteousness of Christ, that is, they receive His redemption, and consequently do not enter the Kingdom, but are cast into eternal torment. So their name is not written in the book of life, that is, they have no portion with Christ, and consequently are deprived of the communion of the saints.

69.17.3.en: Do not be lax with evil, for your God is long-suffering and of great mercy, and He is also just, and repays for every evil thought, word and deed. Do not defy God with your sins, but on the contrary return to Him with repentance and humility and He will receive you. And do not be troubled by your weakness, for He loves the weak and supports them, and rescues them from every sin.

69.18.s.en: (5) Praise of God the Savior of His children

69.18.0.en: 29- But I am poor and sorrowful: let thy salvation, O God, set me up on high.

69.18.1.en: After all the sufferings that David met, he did not answer them with any wrong; he did not meet violence with violence, but bore them with humility and spiritual poverty, and the signs of pain and depression covered his face. And when he accepted these sufferings for the sake of God, He blessed him with many spiritual blessings. The first is mentioned in this verse, and it is his salvation that lifts David from his sufferings; that is, David believed in God the Savior, so his heart was lifted up and he lived in hope. And indeed God saved him from the hand of Saul, then from the hand of Absalom, and from the hand of everyone who wanted to wrong him. David's greatest hope was in Christ who was to come in the fullness of time to lift him from hell to Paradise. David lived in hope, so his heart was lifted up in joy.

69.19.0.en: 30- I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. 31- This also shall please the Lord better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs.

69.19.1.en: Shall please: becomes a good offering with which God is pleased.

69.19.3.en: The second blessing that God gives to His righteous children who endure sufferings for His sake is that they praise Him, magnify Him, and thank Him for His salvation. This praise has great value in God's sight, because it is praise despite the sufferings they endured, and because they tasted and experienced fellowship with God through the affliction, so they praised Him and glorified Him. The value of this praise in God's sight is greater than all animal sacrifices and offerings, even if the sacrifice is as great as an ox.

69.20.0.en: 32- The humble shall see this, and be glad: and your heart shall live that seek God. 33- For the Lord heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners.

69.20.1.en: 1- The third blessing that God gives to the righteous who endure sufferings is joy, for their hearts rejoice in fellowship with God and His work in them, and His rescuing them from their enemies.

69.20.2.en: 2- As for the fourth blessing, it is life with God, while they are on earth, then eternal life in the Kingdom. He gives it to everyone who suffers pains and takes refuge in God with many requests, for He regards their requests and answers them, and frees them from the slavery of the world if they were enslaved, and from the slavery of sin, so they live with Him and enjoy fellowship with Him, and from the captivity of the body, so they put it off, and depart in the spirit, and rejoice in heaven. Also everyone who clung to God and became a prisoner of His love, like St. Paul the Apostle (Phil 1:1), to enjoy life with God.

69.21.0.en: 34- Let the heaven and earth praise him, the seas, and every thing that moveth therein. 35- For God will save Zion, and will build the cities of Judah: that they may dwell there, and have it in possession. 36- The seed also of his servants shall inherit it: and they that love his name shall dwell therein.

69.21.1.en: 1- The fifth blessing is the praise of the whole creation to God, sharing with the righteous man who endured sufferings for God, so he sees all creation around him sharing his praise: the heavens and all that is in them of angels, and the earth and all that is on it of human beings, animals and plants, and likewise the seas and all the animals that move in them; all these walk in their order in submission to God, and are led after man, the greatest creature, the leader of the praise of God.

69.21.2.en: 2- The sixth blessing is the gift of salvation for Zion and Judah and those who dwell in them, and that is through the salvation accomplished in the fullness of time by Christ the Redeemer, when He founds His Church in every place, so His children find a dwelling and stability in her, and live to God, not only in one temple in the world, that is, in Jerusalem, but in every place. For Christ, although His salvation went out from Jerusalem, spreads His churches throughout the world, and the righteous who endured sufferings with thanksgiving and continued seeking God, and all the prisoners of His love, dwell in them, as we mentioned in the previous verses (vv. 32, 33). The righteous who walked in the way of their righteous fathers also enjoy life in the Church, which is the icon of heaven, or the new Zion, and the heavenly Jerusalem.

69.21.3.en: God's gifts to you are renewed every day, so the least you can do is thank Him and praise Him, and your heart will rejoice and you will enjoy fellowship with Him, and your heart will cling to the Kingdom of Heaven.

69.21.4.en: The salvation of the righteous and the shame of the wicked. To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance. "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O Lord" (v. 1) Introduction:

69.21.7.en: When David was exposed to a severe trial, perhaps it was Saul's pursuit of him, or Absalom's driving him out, or any other trial.

69.21.8.en: 3- We see in the title the phrase "to bring to remembrance," that is, reminding God to intervene for David's great need of Him.

69.21.9.en: 4- This psalm suits every person in distress, so that he may be strengthened and his adherence to God may increase.

69.21.10.en: 5- This psalm is liturgical, that is, it is prayed in communal prayer, and most likely at the time of offering incense in the sanctuary.

69.21.11.en: 6- In terms of meaning, this psalm is considered an extension of Psalm 69 and an introduction to Psalm 71; these three psalms ask for salvation from God because of severe distress.

69.21.12.en: 7- There is a strong similarity between this psalm and Psalm 40, for the five verses of Psalm 70 are repeated in the verses (Ps 40:13-17) with a few verbal differences that do not change the general meaning of each verse.

69.21.13.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Prime prayer of the Agpeya, because the one praying begins his day by asking God's help, so that he may face any afflictions he may meet.

69.21.14.en: Note: refer to the commentary on (Ps 40:13-17) found in Volume Ten of the Church Encyclopedia. And we offer you, dear reader, here a brief commentary on each verse.
